goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:224 — Existing client resources are evaluated without CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so an object-level allow can bypass an all-clients deny policy.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) method at line 224, when a specific client resource is found (resource != null after findByName), it proceeds to evaluate permissions on that resource. When no specific resource is found, it falls back to checking the CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE resource. The finding claims that object-level allow can bypass all-clients deny, but the code actually checks for specific client resources first, and only falls back to the type-level resource when no specific resource exists. This is the expected behavior for fine-grained permissions - specific permissions should take precedence. The code doesn't show a bug where deny policies are bypassed; it shows standard permission evaluation logic.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo() at line 148 throws UnsupportedOperationException unconditionally. This method is part of the ClientPermissionEvaluator interface and would be called during token exchange operations. When FGAP v2 is enabled (via MgmtPermissionsV2 returning ClientPermissionsV2), any token exchange attempt would hit this method and throw an exception, resulting in HTTP 500 errors rather than proper authorization denial. The finding correctly identifies that this creates a path where authenticated requests can trigger server errors.

This is a real defect - the method should either be properly implemented or the feature should be disabled/handled gracefully rather than throwing an exception.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — The lookup filters by server ID even though per-client resources are owned by the server client ID, so client-specific permissions are never evaluated.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 214 in ClientPermissionsV2.java, the code is `Resource resource = resourceStore.findByName(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, server.getId());`. This is looking up the 'Clients' resource type resource (the all-clients resource), not a per-client resource. The server.getId() as the third parameter is correct for finding the resource type resource owned by the server. The finding misunderstands the purpose of this method - hasPermission(String scope) is checking for permissions on all clients, not a specific client. For specific client permissions, hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) is used which correctly looks up by client.getId() first.

Without seeing the parent class implementation, the claim about a missing guard cannot be verified from this diff.

If V1 token exchange code paths call this method when V2 permissions are active (via MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returning ClientPermissionsV2), it will throw an exception instead of returning a proper allow/deny decision. The parent class ClientPermissions has a working implementation, but V2 explicitly throws. This could break existing token exchange functionality when the new admin permissions feature is enabled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:148 — Subclassing ClientPermissions while rejecting twelve inherited operations exposes a partially valid object whose unsupported surface is discoverable only at runtime.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ClientPermissionsV2 extends ClientPermissions and overrides 12 methods to throw UnsupportedOperationException (lines 148-195). This is a valid architectural concern - the class inherits a public interface but rejects many operations at runtime. However, this is a design decision for V2 permissions, not a bug. The methods are clearly marked as 'Not supported in V2' and the class is specifically for the V2 permission system. This is an important design consideration but not a defect - it's intentional behavior for a transitional/versioned API.

All three methods contain similar logic for evaluating permissions and scanning scopes with nested loops. This is a valid code duplication concern that could lead to inconsistent changes in the future. However, this is a design/maintainability issue rather than a bug - the code functions correctly as written.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/AbstractPermissionTest.java:136 — The newly generalized createClientPolicy helper has no callers and should be removed until a test needs it.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims createClientPolicy has no callers, but examining the diff shows it IS called in PermissionClientTest.java at line 135: 'UserPolicyRepresentation onlyMyAdminUserPolicy = createUserPolicy(realm, client, "Only My Admin User Policy", myadmin.getId());' and the createClientPolicy method could be used for future tests. More importantly, looking at the test file PermissionClientTest.java, while createUserPolicy is used extensively, createClientPolicy is indeed defined but the diff doesn't show it being called. However, this is a test helper method that provides symmetry with createUserPolicy and follows the pattern of the codebase. Removing unused test utilities is a minor style concern, not an important issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — getClientsWithPermission scans every client resource and performs a full authorization evaluation per resource, creating an unbounded N+1 path

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getClientsWithPermission() in ClientPermissionsV2.java iterates over all resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and calls hasGrantedPermission() for each one, which performs a full authorization evaluation (root.evaluatePermission()). This is an O(N) operation where N is the number of client resources, and each iteration involves policy evaluation. This is a legitimate performance/scalability concern for the new code, though it's not a bug per se - the code will function correctly, just potentially slowly with many clients. The pattern is visible in lines 130-140 of the new file.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:65 — Per-client and all-clients manage grants omit the inherited internal-client guard, allowing delegated admins to modify the realm-management client.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, ClientPermissionsV2.canManage(ClientModel client) at line 65 checks only `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS)` or `hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. Comparing to the parent class ClientPermissions (not fully shown but referenced), the V1 implementation likely includes a guard against modifying internal clients like realm-management. The V2 implementation appears to omit this protection, which could allow delegated admins with manage permission on a specific client to potentially modify protected internal clients. However, I cannot fully verify this without seeing the parent class implementation. The finding is plausible given the pattern of V2 classes simplifying permission checks.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:65 — Granting manage solely from the target-client permission lets delegated admins attach or remove client scopes they cannot view or manage, injecting their mappers and roles into issued tokens.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that granting 'manage' permission on a client allows delegated admins to attach/remove client scopes they cannot view or manage. However, looking at the diff, the canManage(ClientModel client) method at line 65 checks for MANAGE_CLIENTS admin role OR the MANAGE permission on the specific client. The client scope operations (addDefaultClientScope, removeDefaultClientScope, etc.) are tested in the test file and work correctly with MANAGE permission. The finding assumes a security flaw where client scope permissions are bypassed, but the diff doesn't show evidence of this - the permission model appears to be working as designed where MANAGE on a client grants full management capabilities for that client. The finding is speculative about a cross-resource permission bypass that isn't demonstrated in the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:78 — The global canView shortcut bypasses a negative per-client view permission, exposing clients that an explicit object-level policy denies.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel client) at line 78-82: it returns true if canView() returns true (which checks global VIEW permission) OR canConfigure(client) returns true. The issue is that canView() at line 85-87 checks for global VIEW permission without considering per-client negative permissions. In contrast, the test UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testViewUserPermissionDenyByDefault shows the expected pattern where a negative per-client permission should override a positive global permission. However, in ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel), if canView() returns true (global permission), it short-circuits and returns true without checking if there's a negative per-client permission via hasPermission(client, VIEW). This is inconsistent with the user permission model shown in the tests and could expose clients that should be denied by explicit negative policies.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — Gating deletion cleanup on the V1 feature leaves V2 client authorization resources orphaned, so a recreated client with the same ID inherits stale grants.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the event listener in AdminPermissions.registerListener() now wraps all cleanup logic (for roles, clients, groups) inside a check for `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)`. This is the V1 feature flag. Looking at the new V2 implementation (ClientPermissionsV2), it creates resources in the authorization store (via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource and resourceStore operations). When a client is removed, the ClientRemovedEvent would trigger cleanup via `management().clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)`, but this is now gated on the V1 feature flag. If V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the cleanup won't run, leaving orphaned authorization resources. When a new client is created with the same ID, it could inherit these stale permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:101 — Add an integration test for map-roles-client-scope because this new authorization path is never exercised.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to line 101 in ClientPermissionsV2.java which implements canMapClientScopeRoles() using AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. Looking at the test file PermissionClientTest.java, the testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient test only tests MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE scopes, but does not test MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. This is a valid observation - new authorization logic was added but the specific MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE path is not covered by the tests in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:359 — Grant map-roles and map-roles-composite separately because the combined grant lets swapped or overbroad scope checks pass unnoticed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a test design concern in testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient() at line 359. The test creates a single permission with Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE) combined together. The reviewer suggests that granting these scopes separately would provide better test coverage to detect if scope checks are swapped or overbroad. This is a valid test quality concern - combining all scopes in one permission means the test wouldn't catch if canMapRoles() accidentally checked MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE instead of MAP_ROLES. However, this is a test improvement suggestion rather than a bug, as the current test does verify the basic functionality works.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:82 — Add a per-client view test because existing coverage only grants view on the all-clients resource and never exercises this object-specific branch.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new `canView(ClientModel client)` method in `ClientPermissionsV2.java` at line 82 has a branch `hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW)` that checks view permission on a specific client resource. Looking at the test file `PermissionClientTest.java`, the tests use `createAllPermission(client, clientsType, ...)` which grants permissions on the all-clients resource type, not on individual client resources. The `testManageOnlyOneClient` test does create a permission for a specific client but only for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. There's no test that creates a VIEW permission for a specific client to exercise the object-specific view branch in `canView(ClientModel client)`. This is a valid observation about missing test coverage for newly added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:106 — Add realm client-scope read and mutation tests because client default-scope operations do not exercise the new ClientScopeModel authorization methods.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new ClientPermissionsV2 class with canManage(ClientScopeModel) and canView(ClientScopeModel) methods at lines 106-113. The finding correctly identifies that while PermissionClientTest.java adds tests for client permissions (testManageOnlyOneClient, testConfigureOnlyOneClient, testManageAllClients, testViewAllClients, testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient), there are no tests specifically exercising the ClientScopeModel authorization methods. The test file does test client default scope operations (removeDefaultClientScope, addOptionalClientScope) but these test the client-level permissions, not the ClientScopeModel-specific canManage/canView methods. This is a valid observation about missing test coverage for newly added authorization logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — Add V1 and V2 deletion-event tests because the new feature gate changes role client and group permission cleanup without any regression coverage.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the event listener in AdminPermissions.java now wraps all deletion-event handling (RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, GroupRemovedEvent) inside a feature flag check for ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ. This is a behavioral change - previously these cleanup operations ran unconditionally, now they only run when the feature is enabled. The finding correctly identifies that this change lacks test coverage. Looking at the test files in the diff, there are no tests specifically verifying that permission cleanup occurs correctly when roles/clients/groups are deleted under both V1 and V2 scenarios. This is a legitimate concern about missing regression coverage for a meaningful behavioral change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:175 — Create a permission using a public clientId because all added tests use internal IDs and leave the new clientId fallback unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `resolveClient` method at line 175 that includes fallback logic: first it tries `getClientById(realm, id)`, and if that returns null, it falls back to `getClientByClientId(realm, id)`. Looking at all the test cases in `PermissionClientTest.java`, they consistently use internal IDs (e.g., `myclient.getId()`, `realmClient.getId()`) when creating permissions. The finding correctly identifies that the clientId fallback path (the second branch in resolveClient) is never exercised by the tests. This is a valid test coverage gap for newly added logic.
